They are sometimes appropriate in extreme, intractable cases (for example, a dog headed for the shelter) or when an animal is causing harm to himself.

They can also be beneficial as an interim measure to interrupt the cycle of behavior at the same time other less harmful remedies are being attempted. Behavior modification along with a wide variety of natural remedies is generally recommended first, since every drug has side effects.

In a post in the Whole Dog Journal, professional trainer Mardi Richmond discusses additional treatment strategies such as avoiding known triggers, interrupting and redirecting the compulsive behavior, teaching an alternative response, and creating a structured daily routine (to reduce stress).

It’s also important not to try to prevent a dog from performing a repetitive behavior with physical restraint, because it typically causes more anxiety, not less.

item.title: Is Your Pet's Brain Aging Faster Than Their Body?

  • As dogs and cats live longer, more of them are developing cognitive dysfunction, which can show up as confusion, nighttime pacing, altered sleep-wake cycles, forgotten routines, and reduced responsiveness to familiar cues
  • Lion's Mane (Hericium erinaceus) is an edible medicinal mushroom containing bioactive compounds that stimulate nerve growth factor (NGF), a protein essential for the growth, maintenance, and repair of neurons throughout the brain and nervous system
  • Beyond cognitive support, Lion's Mane offers a rare combination of benefits — reducing brain inflammation, fighting oxidative stress, feeding beneficial gut bacteria (a link to the gut-brain axis), modulating immunity, and supporting peripheral nerve regeneration
  • Human trials show improved cognitive scores in adults with mild cognitive impairment after 16 weeks of Lion's Mane, and a 2022 canine study found meaningful favorable shifts in the gut microbiome of aged dogs receiving the mushroom for 16 weeks — though direct cognitive trials in dogs and cats are still emerging
  • Lion's Mane has an excellent safety profile with rare mild side effects (loose stool, brief lethargy); typical prevention dosing is around 1/4 teaspoon per 10 pounds of body weight daily, and consistency over 2 to 4 weeks matters more than any single dose

Your senior dog can still trot around the block. Your senior cat still jumps up to their favorite windowsill. Physically, they seem to be doing okay for their age. But if you look closer, you will see signs that something quieter has changed.

You may notice your dog wandering into corners and forgetting why they went there. Or your cat might start crying in the middle of the night, while staring at a wall. They pace at night. They seem foggy sometimes, or a little more anxious than they used to be. The body is holding up, but the mind seems to be aging on its own timeline.

This mismatch is more common than most pet parents realize, and as dogs and cats live longer, we are seeing more of it. And one of the most talked-about natural supports for the aging pet brain is a shaggy, unusual-looking mushroom called Lion’s Mane.

When the Body Outlasts the Brain

As pets age, they can develop something similar to Alzheimer’s or age-related dementia in humans. In dogs, this is called canine cognitive dysfunction, sometimes referred to as “doggie dementia.” Cats have their own version as well.

Early signs of cognitive dysfunction can be easy to miss or may be dismissed as “just getting old.” They may include:1,2,3

  • Confusion, getting stuck in corners or behind furniture, or standing in the wrong room
  • Wandering, especially at night
  • Restlessness or altered sleep-wake cycles
  • Increased anxiety or irritability
  • Appetite changes, often showing up as an increased appetite or appetite for foods the pet would not eat previously
  • Less interest in play, toys, or familiar people
  • Forgotten commands, cues, or household routines
  • Vocalizing more, especially at odd hours
  • Reduced responsiveness when called by name

Cognitive dysfunction is not something to panic about, but it is worth naming. Once you can see it, you can start doing something about it — and Lion’s Mane is one of the tools that keeps coming up in that conversation.4

What Lion’s Mane Actually Is

Lion’s Mane (Hericium erinaceus) is an edible medicinal mushroom native to hardwood forests in North America, Europe, and Asia. It gets its name from its white, shaggy, cascading appearance that really does look a bit like a lion’s mane.5 It has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries to “nourish the gut and calm the mind.” Buddhist monks reportedly drank Lion’s Mane tea before meditation to sharpen their focus. What is newer is the growing body of research trying to understand exactly how it works.

Lion’s Mane contains a set of bioactive compounds that make it interesting for brain health. Two in particular — hericenones and erinacines — are believed to stimulate the production of nerve growth factor (NGF), a protein essential for the growth, maintenance, and repair of nerve cells.6,7 It also contains beta-glucan polysaccharides, isoindolinones, sterols, and antioxidants that appear to have neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects.8

How It Works

Lion’s Mane’s most celebrated action is its ability to support brain health from multiple directions at once. Rather than a singular effect, it appears to work simultaneously on nerve growth, inflammation, oxidative stress, and gut function — which is a rare profile for a single natural ingredient:9,10

  • Encouraging NGF production — NGF helps neurons grow, survive, and repair themselves. In animal studies, Lion’s Mane compounds have been shown to help regenerate myelin along damaged nerve fibers11 — the insulation that helps nerves conduct signals properly.
  • Reducing brain inflammation — Chronic low-grade inflammation in the brain is a driver of age-related decline. Lion’s Mane has demonstrated anti-inflammatory activity in the nervous system in a range of studies.
  • Fighting oxidative stress — The compounds in Lion's Mane are antioxidant-rich, which may help to neutralize the free radicals that damage brain cells over time.
  • Supporting the gut-brain axis — Lion’s Mane also acts as a prebiotic, feeding beneficial gut bacteria. Since roughly 70% to 80% of the immune system lives in the digestive tract, and gut health increasingly appears to influence brain health, this matters.

Together, these effects make Lion's Mane one of the more compelling natural options for comprehensively supporting an aging brain — not as a cure, but as a multi-front helper.

What the Research Actually Shows

Most of the strongest research on Lion's Mane comes from preclinical trials, limited human trials, and lab studies in rodents. Direct research in dogs and cats is still emerging. Here is what the evidence looks like right now.

  • In human trials with adults who had mild cognitive impairment, taking Lion’s Mane daily for 16 weeks led to significantly improved cognitive scores compared to placebo.12 Notably, when subjects stopped taking it, those improvements faded — suggesting consistent use is what maintains the benefit.13
  • A separate 12-week clinical trial in humans found that Lion’s Mane safely enhanced cognitive function on memory and recognition tests.14 A small study also found reductions in anxiety and depression in adults taking Lion’s Mane for four weeks.15
  • In canines specifically, a 2022 peer-reviewed study fed aged dogs a diet supplemented with Lion’s Mane for 16 weeks. The dogs receiving the mushroom showed meaningful, favorable shifts in their gut microbiome — beneficial bacteria increased and harmful bacteria decreased. Researchers concluded that Lion’s Mane could “regulate the gut microbial community in aged dogs,” with potential downstream benefits for immunity and metabolic health.16

Formal cognitive trials in dogs are limited so far, but many integrative veterinarians report seeing improvements in their aging patients — better alertness, calmer nights, more engagement — after several weeks of Lion’s Mane. That is real-world observation, not controlled data, but it is consistent with what the underlying science suggests.

Beyond the Brain

While cognitive support is the headliner, Lion’s Mane has a wide-ranging list of other potential effects that make it appealing for senior pets.17,18

  • Immune modulation, thanks to its beta-glucans
  • Anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties
  • Gut and digestive support, including prebiotic effects
  • Support for peripheral nerve regeneration
  • Blood sugar regulation in animal studies19,20
  • Cardiovascular and metabolic support

This is one reason integrative veterinarians increasingly reach for Lion’s Mane in older dogs and cats. It touches many of the systems that quietly wear down with age at the same time.

Who Might Benefit

Lion's Mane is not just for pets who already have obvious cognitive decline. It is also being used preventively for senior animals whose brains are still working well but who are entering a life stage where support matters. Situations where a veterinarian might consider Lion's Mane include:

  • Senior dogs or cats showing early signs of cognitive change
  • Older pets with anxiety, especially nighttime restlessness
  • Pets with peripheral nerve issues or degenerative myelopathy
  • Recovery from spinal cord injuries or disc disease
  • Chronic gut issues, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), or gastritis
  • Immune support, including as part of an integrative cancer care plan
  • General wellness support for aging animals eating a diet you would like to enrich

This is not a supplement to hand out casually. It is a tool with real biological effects that deserves a conversation with your vet — especially if your pet is on medications or has existing health conditions.

Safety and Side Effects

Lion’s Mane has an excellent safety profile in the research so far. Rodent toxicology studies have used extraordinarily high doses for months without adverse effects, and no serious side effects have been documented in dogs, cats, or humans consuming it long-term. When side effects do happen in pets, they are usually mild and short-lived:21,22,23

  • Loose stool or soft stool when first starting
  • Mild digestive upset, especially at higher doses on an empty stomach
  • Occasional lethargy during the first few days

A few situations warrant extra caution and a veterinary conversation before starting. Do not give Lion’s Mane if your pet is:

  • Allergic to mushrooms (rare but real)
  • Being given blood thinners or NSAIDs, since Lion’s Mane may slightly affect clotting
  • Taking immunosuppressive drugs or have certain autoimmune conditions, since Lion’s Mane stimulates the immune system
  • Pregnant or nursing, where safe use has not been established

Bring a list of your pet's medications and supplements to the conversation. Natural does not automatically mean interaction-free.

Dosage Basics

Dosing depends on your pet's size, the concentration of the product, and the reason you are using it. In an Animal Wellness Magazine article, the late Ihor J. Basko, DVM, CVA, shared his common integrative-vet guidelines for powdered Lion’s Mane extract:24

  • Prevention or general support — 1/4 teaspoon per 10 pounds body weight, given once daily
  • Active health concern — 1/2 teaspoon per 10 pounds body weight, given twice daily

For extract capsules, a rough range often used is around 20 to 40 milligrams (mg) per kilogram of body weight per day. Practically, that lands at roughly 250 mg to 500 mg for a 25-pound dog, 500 mg to 1,000 mg for a 50-pound dog, and 750 mg to 1,500 mg or more for larger breeds.25 Here are a few tips that make dosing easier:

  • Start low and build up over three to five days.
  • Give it with meals to improve absorption and reduce GI upset.
  • Mix powder into warm bone broth or wet food if the taste is a barrier.
  • Stay consistent — the effects fade if you stop, so daily use is the goal.

Most owners start noticing subtle changes within two to four weeks. Some pets take longer. Consistency matters more than any single dose.

What to Look for in a Lion’s Mane Supplement

Mushroom supplements vary wildly in quality. If you are going to use Lion’s Mane, spending a little more on a good product is worth it. Keep in mind these tips:26,27

  • Fruiting body vs. mycelium — The fruiting body is the actual mushroom. Mycelium is the root-like network, often grown on grain. Some cheap supplements are almost entirely mycelium-on-grain, meaning most of what’s in the bottle is starch, not mushroom. Look for products labeled 100% fruiting body.
  • Extraction — Hot-water and dual (hot water plus alcohol) extractions pull out the active compounds much more efficiently than raw powdered mushrooms. Extracts tend to be more potent per gram.
  • Beta-glucan content — A quality Lion’s Mane product will disclose its beta-glucan percentage, ideally somewhere in the 20% to 40% range. Vague labels that only mention “polysaccharides” can hide a lot of filler starch.
  • Third-party testing — Look for organic sourcing and independent testing for heavy metals, pesticides, and microbial contamination.
  • Free of harmful additives — Skip anything with sweeteners like xylitol (highly toxic to dogs) or unfamiliar flavor blends. A pet-specific supplement or a plain, unflavored powder is usually the safest bet.
  • Proper packaging — Dark or opaque containers protect the mushroom from light degradation. Check expiration dates.

Setting Realistic Expectations

Lion's Mane is not a miracle cure. It will not reverse advanced dementia, and it does not replace veterinary care for serious conditions, but it may help support the aging brain in a meaningful, low-risk way.

Pet parents with older canine companions often notice effects such as seeming more “present” during the day, less pacing at night, better recognition of familiar people, easier settling into sleep, and slightly more spark than the weeks before. It is nothing dramatic, but it is real and cumulative over time.

This is a supplement that pairs beautifully with the other pillars of senior pet care: high-quality nutrition, regular veterinary checkups (at least twice yearly for older pets), mental enrichment, gentle daily exercise, weight management, and a calm home environment. It complements those areas of health — it does not replace them.

The Bigger Picture

Watching a beloved pet's body outlast their sharpness is one of the harder parts of loving them into their later years. The confusion, the wandering, the little forgotten things — none of it means you are losing them all at once. It just means their brain is entering the same aging conversation their joints and eyes and heart already know.

Lion's Mane is not the answer to every part of that. But it is one of the few natural options with a plausible biological mechanism, a good safety record, and a growing body of supportive research. That combination is rare in the world of supplements.

If your pet is starting to feel a little foggier than they used to, talk to your veterinarian. Ask about Lion's Mane specifically. Ask about a quality product, an appropriate dose, and a reasonable timeline for seeing whether it helps. And keep supporting all the other things — enrichment, food, checkups, and connection — that also help an old brain stay a little sharper for a little longer.

Your pet has been paying close attention to you for their whole life. Returning that attention now, when the wiring is starting to slow, is one of the kindest things you can offer them.

  • 2,8,10,17,22,24 Animal Wellness Magazine, March 23, 2026
  • 3,7,23,26 Woof Doctor on Wheels, Exploring the Benefits of Lion’s Mane Mushroom for Senior Dogs and Cats
  • 11 Sci Rep. 2021 Mar 22;11:6551, Results
  • 12 Phytother Res. 2009 Mar;23(3):367-72
  • 13 Nutrients. 2023 Nov 20;15(22):4842
  • 14 Biomedical Research 40(4):125-131, August 2019
  • 15 Biomed Res. 2010 Aug;31(4):231-7
  • 16 J Anim Sci Technol. 2022 Sep;64(5):937-949
  • 19 Sci Rep. 2017 Sep 7;7:10847
  • 20 Process Biochemistry, Volume 88, January 2020, Pages 180-188

Pet parents with older canine companions often notice effects such as seeming more “present” during the day, less pacing at night, better recognition of familiar people, easier settling into sleep, and slightly more spark than the weeks before. This is a supplement that pairs beautifully with the other pillars of senior pet care: high-quality nutrition, regular veterinary checkups (at least twice yearly for older pets), mental enrichment, gentle daily exercise, weight management, and a calm home environment. It complements those areas of health — it does not replace them.

Watching a beloved pet's body outlast their sharpness is one of the harder parts of loving them into their later years. The confusion, the wandering, the little forgotten things — none of it means you are losing them all at once. It just means their brain is entering the same aging conversation their joints and eyes and heart already know.

Lion's Mane is not the answer to every part of that. But it is one of the few natural options with a plausible biological mechanism, a good safety record, and a growing body of supportive research. That combination is rare in the world of supplements.

If your pet is starting to feel a little foggier than they used to, talk to your veterinarian. Ask about Lion's Mane specifically. Ask about a quality product, an appropriate dose, and a reasonable timeline for seeing whether it helps. And keep supporting all the other things — enrichment, food, checkups, and connection — that also help an old brain stay a little sharper for a little longer.

item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Hairlessness in dogs and cats is a genetic defect that was purposefully propagated at some point in history
  • Hairless dogs and cats may need to be wiped down and/or bathed regularly, because they don’t have fur to absorb all the oil on their skin
  • They are prone to sunburn and are also vulnerable to both hot and cold temperatures
  • Hairless pets are often chosen because they're believed to be hypoallergenic, but no dog or cat is 100% hypoallergenic — allergens are found in saliva, dander and skin, not just fur
  • Popular hairless breeds include the Chinese Crested, Sphynx, Peruvian Inca Orchid, Peterbald and Xoloitzcuintli, each with unique care needs and breed-specific health considerations

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 29, 2016.

You may not be able to imagine your dog or cat without his soft, furry coat, but for some people, a hairless pet is far more alluring. With their unusual and striking appearances, hairless pets attract a lot of attention, but it's their personalities that make a lasting mark on their owners' hearts.

Hairlessness in dogs and cats is actually a genetic defect that was purposefully propagated at some point in history.

Today, while some people choose hairless pets simply because they like their appearance, they're most often chosen over their furry counterparts because they do not shed and are assumed to be hypoallergenic (which isn't necessarily the case — more on this later).

Skin Problems Are More Likely in Hairless Pets

There are some special considerations if you share your life with a hairless dog or cat, especially when it comes to caring for their skin.

Hairless cats may need to be wiped down or even bathed regularly, because they don't have fur to absorb all the oil on their skin. Hairless dogs need regular baths too — typically once a week or every other week.

If you don't bathe them often enough, they may develop acne, but if you bathe them too often or with the wrong shampoo (best to use an organic, coconut-oil-based shampoo with no harsh chemicals) their skin may become dry and irritated. Coconut oil makes a good post-bath moisturizer.

Skin infections can be common in hairless pets, including yeast overgrowth in cats. You'll also need to protect your dog from the elements even more so than a fur-covered pet.

They are prone to sunburn (consider the use of an animal-friendly natural sunscreen when your pet will be outdoors for longer periods) and are also vulnerable to both hot and cold temperatures, as fur helps regulate the skin's surface temperature.

Hairless dogs living in cold climates should wear a coat when they go outdoors and may also enjoy wearing a soft sweater when they're inside.

Are Hairless Dogs and Cats a Good Choice for People with Allergies?

Aside from the fact that they don't shed (or shed only slightly in those with tufts of hair), the other common reason why people choose hairless dogs and cats is because they're believed to be hypoallergenic.

However, there are no 100% hypoallergenic cats or dogs. This is because the major cat and dog allergens (Can f 1 [dog allergen] and Fel d 1 [cat allergen]) are found not only in hair but also in saliva and dander and on the skin.

For instance, all cats produce the Fel d 1 protein, and it's not related to the amount of dander or shedding. The Fel d 1 protein is quite small, so when it's attached to a piece of airborne cat skin, it can linger in the air for hours.

Some of the best cats for people with allergies therefore have nothing to do with how much fur they have but with how much Fel d 1 protein they produce. The Balinese, which has a long shaggy coat, is actually one of the most "hypoallergenic" cat breeds because they produce less Fel d 1 protein than other breeds.

That being said, with no fur to trap allergens from their saliva, hairless cats and dogs may not cause an allergic reaction as easily as other breeds. Keep in mind, however, that even without fur the Fel d 1 (or Can f 1) protein will still be present.

5 Hairless Cat and Dog Breeds

There are several types of hairless dogs and cats. Each breed is as unique as its appearance implies.

  1. Chinese Crested (Dog) — Chinese Crested dogs may be hairless or coated (known as powderpuffs). The hairless type has a mohawk-like strip of fur on his head and long fur on his ears, face, tail, feet and lower legs. Chinese Cresteds are intelligent, agile and affectionate dogs who love to be with their owners.

    Chinese Crested may be at increased risk of inherited eye diseases, including progressive retinal atrophy and primary lens luxation, which may cause vision loss. They are also prone to developing blackheads and other acne and may suffer from dental abnormalities.
  2. Sphynx (Cat) — The Sphynx is a cross between hairless cats and rex cats. They're known for their large ears and wrinkly skin, which requires regular bathing or wipe downs because it's rich in oils. Some Sphynx cats have fine "peach fuzz" like fur while others may feel like suede.

    These cats tend to crave attention and like to show off for their owners. They're affectionate and often engage in silly antics. Aside from the potential for clogged pores in their skin, Sphynx cats are not prone to any serious health problems.
  3. Peruvian Inca Orchid (Dog) — This exotic-sounding dog is a cousin to the Chinese Crested. He's a sighthound who is born without fur except for a small patch atop his head as well as on his toes and tip of his tail.

    Peruvian Inca Orchids tend to be loyal and affectionate dogs with a playful nature and good manners. They are not prone to any specific medical problems.
  4. Peterbald (Cat) — Peterbalds, which originated in St. Petersburg, Russia, come in four coat types ranging from hairless with slightly sticky skin (known as ultrabald) to "brush coat," which describes a variety of hair that may be fine, long, wiry or a combination.

    Peterbalds are affectionate, intelligent and extroverted cats that may vocalize loudly. The genetic mutation that causes hairlessness may be a cause of feline ectodermal dysplasia, which is associated with dental abnormalities.
  5. Xoloitzcuintli — Xoloitzcuintlis, or "show-lows" for short, are a primitive breed that originated in Mexico, apparently without much help from humans. Known for being loyal, alert and calm, they're also good watchdogs that are wary of strangers. They tend to be a healthy breed, but may occasionally suffer from kneecap dislocation (luxating patellas).

If you're interested in adding a hairless dog or cat to your family, seek out a pet in need first. Many rescue organizations catering to hairless breeds can be found throughout the U.S. and beyond.

Sources and References

  • 1 AKC, Dog Breeds, Chinese Crested

item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Strawberries can be given as fresh, healthy pet treats or added to your pet's nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet
  • They are rich in flavonoids like anthocyanins, which offer antioxidative and antimicrobial activities, and may have protective effects against several diseases, like heart disease, cancer and diabetes
  • Strawberries contain fisetin, a flavonoid antioxidant that has neurotrophic, anticarcinogenic and anti-inflammatory effects
  • Strawberries also contain an enzyme called malic acid, which acts as a natural whitener for tooth enamel
  • It’s best to buy organic varieties of this fruit as opposed to conventionally grown ones

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 14, 2020.

Strawberries are quintessential and versatile fruits that people add to many kinds of desserts and fresh fruit salads. If you enjoy these berries, you may wonder: Can your pets have them, too? Read further to find out if it's OK for your dogs and cats to eat them, and what benefits they might get from snacking on these fruits.

Yes, Strawberries Are OK for Pets!

Belonging to the rose plant family, the strawberry (Fragaria)1 is one of the most recognizable and well-loved fruits in the world. But despite its name, strawberry isn’t a true berry — rather, it’s considered an accessory fruit, like apples and pears.2 In human health, strawberries are valued for being abundant in “nutritive and non-nutritive bioactive compounds” that may help promote health and reduce the risk of diseases like obesity, cancer, heart disease and diabetes.3

If you love strawberries, then here’s some good news — you can share these juicy, sweet-tart fruits with your dogs and cats (if they’ll have them). They can be given as fresh, healthy pet treats or added to your pet's nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet.

Just make sure you buy organic varieties (more about this later) and slice the fruit in small enough pieces so it will not pose a choking hazard, especially to small-breed dogs. When given as healthy treats, strawberries should make up less than 10% of your pet’s daily caloric intake.

Where Do Strawberries Grow?

Strawberries are native to the Northern Hemisphere, particularly in temperate regions; however, today they are grown all over the world.4 In terms of production, the top three producers are China, the U.S. and Mexico.5

Strawberries Are Rich in Vitamin C and Fisetin

Strawberries are rich in antioxidants, and vitamin C is one of the top nutrients you can get from them. Like most mammals, dogs can make their own vitamin C via their liver,6 but giving them moderate amounts of this nutrient via their diet can still be a boon for their health.

A two tablespoon serving of sliced fresh strawberries can give your pet 12.2 milligrams of this potent vitamin.7 Vitamin C works by scavenging harmful free radicals in your pet’s body.8 It can also inhibit inflammation9 and help slow down cognitive aging.10

Strawberries also contain fisetin, a flavonoid antioxidant that has neurotrophic, anticarcinogenic and anti-inflammatory effects.11 In one study of 40 different food items, strawberries had the highest concentration of fisetin,12 and its promise has been demonstrated for a number of diseases, including diabetes,13 as well as impressive antiaging effects.14

Anthocyanins in Strawberries May Help Support Heart Health

Strawberries are rich in flavonoids, including anthocyanins. This is the most extensive group of water-soluble pigments in the plant kingdom, and they are abundant in berries like blueberries, raspberries and black currants.15 They’re also the reason for the colorful red, orange, blue and violet hues in these plants and other crops.16

According to studies, anthocyanins offer antioxidative and antimicrobial activities, and may have protective effects against several diseases,17 like heart disease,18 cancer19 and diabetes.20 They can also support your pet’s eyesight as well as their neurological health.21

Did You Know?

An average strawberry has 200 seeds — and each seed is considered by botanists to be its own separate fruit!22

Feeding Your Pets Strawberries May Whiten Their Teeth

Giving your pets a few slices of strawberries may also promote good oral health. This is because strawberries contain an enzyme called malic acid, which acts as a natural whitener for tooth enamel. According to a 2018 study, it also “increases saliva production … thereby exerting the anticariogenic property.”23

How to Feed Strawberries to Your Pet

Misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of overconsumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

In the case of strawberries, the green stems and unripened parts of the fruit can cause GI upset, resulting in some websites touting them as being hazardous to pet health, which has confused thousands of pet owners about the safety of strawberries. A good rule of thumb is to feed the same parts of fruits and vegetables to your pets as you feed to the rest of your family (so in this case, no green stems or leaves).

One important thing to remember when feeding your pets strawberries is to give them in moderation, as these fruits still contain sugar, which can be detrimental to your pet’s health in high amounts. As a treat, feed a few (sliced) pieces at a time, or cut the fruit up into small pieces and mix into their meals. Remember to only give them fresh fruit — not strawberry jams or purees, as these have excessive levels of sugar and high fructose corn syrup that can be harmful to your pets.

Did You Know?

The earliest records of strawberries came from ancient Rome, around 200 BC. In the 12th century, Saint Hildegard von Bingen stated that these berries were unfit for consumption as they grow too close to the ground, possibly being contaminated by toads and snakes.


It was only in the mid-18th century when this belief was debunked, thanks to a Swedish botanist named Charles Linnaeus who ate a diet consisting of only strawberries, proving them edible.24

Strawberries Top the Dirty Dozen List, so Buy Them Organic

If you want to feed your pets strawberries, it’s best to buy organic varieties of this fruit as opposed to conventionally grown ones. Strawberries rank No. 3 in the Environmental Working Group’s (EWG) Dirty Dozen list, meaning they are one of the most pesticide-laden crops today. According to an Insider article, “EWG testing revealed that 90% of strawberries contained at least one pesticide, and 30% of the crop had traces of 10 or more different toxins.”25

To keep your pet (and your family) safe from these harmful chemicals, opt for organic or “spray-free” strawberries from local farmers markets.

item.title: Killing Wolves Can Lead to Even More Attacks on Animals
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The U.S. seems to have a love-hate relationship with wolves. A long-standing “solution” to wolf predation of livestock is to shoot them. This “solution” ultimately led to the eradication of wolves across the west
  • Wolves have been reintroduced in several states and have thrived, and once again, wildlife officials and ranchers are shooting them to prevent livestock losses
  • A study concludes that shooting wolves in small numbers actually increases the number of livestock attacks the following year. Only decreasing wolf populations by at least 25% in a single year has an effect
  • Humane solutions do exist and have been used successfully in Idaho, where in 7 years, only 30 sheep have been lost, and no wolves have been shot
  • Killing a wolf pack's breeding pair often causes the pack to disperse, leading to the formation of multiple new breeding pairs and, ultimately, a larger overall wolf population

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 28, 2015.

Wolves are routinely killed in the U.S. to preserve livestock owned by farmers and ranchers. But research suggests that this controversial practice actually may increase the probability that wolves will prey on livestock in the future.

The Washington State University study results were published in December 2014 in the scientific journal PLoS One,1 and they challenge the commonly held notion that the fastest, most efficient method for dealing with wolves that threaten livestock is simply to shoot them.

Wolf packs are multiplying throughout the western states, leaving dead sheep, cattle, and other animals in their wake. Two states now have designated wolf-hunting seasons to address the issue.

It’s inevitable that the new research will add more fuel to the long-standing controversy about how to deal with wolves. "The livestock industry, they're not going to be happy with this," said Rob Wielgus, a Washington State University ecologist and the study's lead author.2

A Schizophrenic Approach to Gray Wolf Management

By the 1930s, open season on gray wolves in the western U.S. had led to their eradication. The animals were reintroduced in the mid-1990s with 66 individuals relocated to Wyoming and Idaho.

Since then the wolves have thrived, to the point where both government wildlife officials and ranchers have resorted to once again shooting them to protect livestock. By 2013, the wolf body count was over 2,000.3

In 2011, in five western states (Idaho, Montana, and parts of Washington, Oregon, and Utah), wolves were removed from federal protection under the Endangered Species Act, making it easier to shoot them. Idaho and Montana even added a wolf season for recreational hunters.

In 2013, hunters killed 356 wolves in Idaho and 231 in Montana, which dropped the population to around 600 in each state. In addition, in 2014 the Idaho legislature created a “Wolf Depredation Control Board” that critics believe will work to take the number of wolves down to just above the cutoff (150) that could again give the animals federal protection under the Endangered Species Act.4

But the question no one was asking was, “Does killing wolves really help protect livestock?”

Study Suggests Killing Small Numbers of Wolves INCREASES Livestock Attacks

Wolves returned to Washington in 2008, and grew to 13 packs by 2013. WSU’s Wielgus, who studies issues of predator control and is the director of WSU’s Large Carnivore Conservation Lab, evaluated a 25-year history of wolf killings and wolf attacks on cattle and sheep in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming, which were the first three states where wolves were reintroduced.

What he discovered was that when a wolf was killed in, say, Idaho, livestock killings in Idaho increased the following year by 5% to 6% for cattle and 4% for sheep. And the number of livestock killed increased with each additional wolf that was shot. If 20 wolves were killed, livestock deaths doubled. The situation didn’t improve until over a quarter of the wolves in the state were killed in a single year. Only then did attacks on livestock begin to decline.

Wielgus suspects the reason more livestock are attacked when smaller numbers of wolves are killed may lie in pack behavior. Wolf packs are headed up by a male and female breeding pair. If one or both are killed, the pack often disperses. Several new breeding pairs are created from that pack, and an increase in the wolf population is the result.

According to the WSU study, livestock attacks decrease only after so many wolves have been killed that they can’t possibly replenish their numbers through reproduction. This actually falls in line with observations made of Yellowstone wolf packs. Packs inside the park, where wolves can’t be shot, are large and complex, and include individuals of varying ages living together, whereas wolf packs living elsewhere consist of just a breeding pair and their pups.

Wielgus believes his study results show that shooting wolves as a routine practice is “counterproductive and unsustainable.”5 Killing small numbers of wolves increases livestock losses, but killing enough wolves to reduce livestock attacks could drive wolf numbers so low that they end up back on the Endangered Species List.

According to the study results, if less than 25% of the wolf population is shot per year, livestock losses increase the following year.

Humane Solutions Exist (and Cost Less Than Sharpshooters in Helicopters)

Predictably, wolf conservationists have welcomed the WSU study results, while the livestock industry persists in its belief that the only way to protect cows and sheep is to kill the wolves that prey on them.

Jamie Henneman of Washington Residents Against Wolves, who is also a spokesperson for the Stevens County Cattlemen’s Association, believes the study results were predetermined to arrive at a pro-wolf conclusion because the research was supported by the State Legislature, which has supported increases in wolf populations.6

But Wielgus feels the anti-wolf groups aren’t really interested in serious wolf management.

“They just want to get rid of wolves,” said Wielgus. “Livestock lobbyists are pretty much vehemently opposed to my research, but in terms of hard science, it stood the test.”7

In searching for humane solutions to the problem, Suzanne Stone of Defenders of Wildlife has worked with ranchers in Idaho on different ways to preserve sheep without killing wolves. Some of the things they’ve tried include:

  • Monitoring the location of wolf dens to avoid grazing sheep in those areas
  • Using guard dogs
  • Increasing the number of herders
  • Flashing bright lights to frighten off the wolves
  • Encircling flocks of sheep at night with wire hung with strips of fabric

The money Stone and the ranchers have spent trying different approaches is less than it costs to send a shooter up in a helicopter. Even better, fewer than 30 sheep have been attacked by wolves in the last 7 years, and no wolves have been killed.

  • 2,3,4,5 National Geographic, December 3, 2014 (Archived)
  • 6,7 New York Times, December 4, 2014

item.title: The Face That Tricks Every Pet Parent
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The classic "guilty look" you see in dogs is almost certainly not actual guilt, according to the best current research; it is a set of appeasement behaviors that they use to de-escalate perceived conflict with their humans
  • A landmark 2009 study found that dogs display "guilty" body language based on how their owners behave, not on whether the dog has actually done anything wrong
  • Guilt is a self-conscious emotion requiring the ability to reflect on past actions and feel remorse, and it is a cognitively complex process not well-supported by current evidence in dogs
  • After-the-fact punishment does not teach dogs anything about their earlier behavior — it just teaches them that owners can be unpredictably scary, sometimes leading to hidden accidents or increased anxiety
  • The effective approach is management, catching them in the act with calm redirection, positive reinforcement, and staying neutral when discovering a mess

You come home, and something is off. Maybe it is the shreds of couch cushion on the floor, or the puddle by the back door, or the pillow that used to have stuffing in it.

Then you see them. Your dog, slinking toward you with head lowered, ears flattened, eyes averted, and a full-body posture that screams: I know I did something bad.

It is one of the most universally recognized expressions in the dog world. And it is also, according to the best current research, almost certainly not what you think it is.

Do Dogs Actually Feel Guilt?

First, let us give dogs the emotional credit they deserve. Research confirms that dogs feel a range of real emotions including joy, fear, love, and anger. Anyone who has lived with one knows this in their bones.

But guilt is a specific and more complex emotion than any of those. In humans, guilt is what psychologists call a self-conscious emotion. It requires the ability to reflect on your own actions, recognize you have broken a rule, and feel remorse about it. That involves a kind of moral self-awareness tied to higher-order thinking.

Shame is a close cousin. In humans, shame is about the self (“I am bad”), while guilt is about the act (“I did something bad”). Neither is well-supported by current evidence as a conscious experience dogs actually have.

What dogs do experience, researchers suggest, is something more immediate and social: a response to cues in their environment, especially the emotional cues coming from their human. That is a quite different mechanism from remorse.1

Some veterinary experts frame this as a classic case of anthropomorphism — the very human tendency to attribute our own characteristics and emotions to animals. It comes from a place of love, but it can also lead us to misread what our dogs are actually telling us.2

The Famous Guilty-Look Study

The most-cited study on this question comes from cognitive scientist Dr. Alexandra Horowitz at Barnard College, published in 2009 in Behavioral Processes.3 Horowitz set up trials in which dog owners either correctly or incorrectly believed their dog had eaten a forbidden treat. She then observed how the dogs behaved when their owners returned. The results were striking.4

Dogs displayed “guilty” behaviors — lowered heads, flattened ears, averted eyes — based on how the owners behaved, not on whether the dog had actually done anything wrong. Innocent dogs who were scolded showed just as much guilty-looking body language as dogs who had truly eaten the treat.5

Horowitz’s conclusion was careful and worth quoting: “A better description of the so-called guilty look is that it is a response to owner cues, rather than that it shows an appreciation of a misdeed.”

Notably, Horowitz herself has said her study was not designed to definitively prove that dogs do not feel guilt. “I would feel dreadful if people then thought the case was closed on dogs (not) feeling guilt, which is definitely not the case,” she said.6

The honest answer, based on the current science, is that the classic guilty look certainly is not guilt — but we cannot say for sure what dogs are subjectively feeling. What we can say is that the face they make when caught has a much simpler explanation.

What the Guilty Look Really Is

What we read as guilt is actually a well-documented set of appeasement behaviors. These are social signals that say, in canine language, “I mean no harm, please don't be angry with me.” The classic guilty look includes some combination of:7,8,9

  • A lowered head
  • Flattened or pinned-back ears
  • Averted eyes or refusal to make eye contact
  • A tucked tail (or a tail thumping the floor from a lowered posture)
  • Lip licking
  • Yawning
  • Whale eye (the whites of the eyes visible)
  • Hunched or lowered body posture
  • Cowering or retreating

These are all appeasement and stress signals. They are deeply ingrained social behaviors inherited from wolves, used to manage relationships and reduce social tension. When your dog senses that you are upset, tense, or angry, they use these signals in an attempt to calm the situation.

Dogs Are Reading You, Not Themselves

Here is what makes this so persuasive. Dogs are extraordinarily skilled at reading human body language, facial expressions, and tone of voice. Research has found they are actually better at reading us than our closest primate relatives are.10

When you walk into a room and your shoulders tense, your brow furrows, and your voice deepens, your dog notices it immediately. They notice the shift long before you have finished processing it consciously. The guilty look is their response to you — not to what they did an hour ago. It is a communication move, not a confession.

Every household has its own set of unwritten rules — what counts as “good” or “bad” behavior varies from home to home. Dogs come into these arrangements with no innate knowledge of your rules. They learn what you prefer through consistent training and consistent consequences, not through some inner moral compass. That is why the same dog can look “guilty” for something that would be perfectly acceptable in another home.11

Why the Look Develops

If the guilty look is not actual guilt, why does it come out so reliably in certain situations? The answer is classical and operant conditioning — the same learning mechanisms that shape most dog behavior.

Dogs are pattern-recognition experts. Over time, they learn to associate specific situations with specific outcomes. A dog who has been scolded for coming home to find a chewed-up cushion starts to associate coming home + chewed-up cushion + owner arriving with a negative reaction.

Crucially, the dog is not connecting their earlier chewing with the punishment. They are connecting the current environmental context (owner arriving, mess on floor) with what usually happens next (unpleasant interaction).

Over time, with repetition, that anticipation becomes a reliable, conditioned response. The guilty look then shows up preemptively any time those conditions are present — regardless of whether the dog has actually done anything wrong.

This helps explain some real-life head-scratchers. In multi-dog households, sometimes the guilty-looking dog is the innocent one — the peacemaker of the pair, who reads the tension and tries to de-escalate.12,13

Dogs Live in the Present

Another piece of the puzzle is time. Dogs live largely in the moment. They can have impressive memories for people, places, and trained behaviors, but their ability to consciously reflect on a past action and connect it to a delayed consequence is quite limited.

Studies on canine cognition suggest dogs have extremely limited deferred learning — meaning they struggle to link a consequence to an action that happened more than a few seconds earlier. The scold that happens two hours after the cushion was chewed simply does not connect back to the chewing in the dog's mind.

A dog who chewed a shoe two hours ago is not sitting in the corner thinking about it. They are doing dog things. Then you walk in, and their reaction is to your body language in the moment — not to the chewed shoe.14,15

Why After-the-Fact Punishment Backfires

This has real, practical consequences. Scolding your dog after the fact does not teach them not to chew shoes. It teaches them that their owner sometimes becomes unpredictably scary. That is the opposite of what most pet parents want.

Research on dog training outcomes has consistently shown that punishment-based methods are associated with increased anxiety, fear, and aggression — without producing reliable improvement in unwanted behavior.16

And there is a subtle side effect worth understanding. If you repeatedly react with anger to a mess (say, an accident on the rug), your dog learns to fear the presence of the mess itself. Some dogs start hiding accidents — eliminating in the basement or behind furniture — not because they know it is wrong, but because they have learned that your reaction to a visible mess is unpleasant.

Here’s What to Do Instead

Once you understand what the guilty look is, you can respond in ways that will help. Here are a few evidence-backed strategies:17,18,19

  • Focus on management first — Prevent access to the things your dog gets into. Crate training, baby gates, closed doors, and putting temptations out of reach do more than any correction can. Dogs cannot destroy what they cannot reach.
  • Only intervene if you catch them in the act — There is a two-second rule that helps: If you did not see it happen and cannot interrupt it in the moment, let it go. Redirecting a dog mid-behavior, such as offering an appropriate toy to chew and rewarding chewing on the toy, is far more effective than after-the-fact scolding.
  • Reinforce what you want — Positive reinforcement (rewarding desired behavior with treats, praise, or play) is the most effective and least harmful method of shaping dog behavior. Rather than focusing on what your dog did wrong, focus on building the habits you want them to have.
  • Supervise, then interrupt calmly — When your dog is wandering and eyeing something they should not have, gently interrupt them before it becomes a chase. A shake of a treat bag, a squeaked toy, a friendly call — all followed by a reward when they redirect to you.
  • Stay calm when you find a mess — This is often the hardest part. Try to remember that your emotional response is what your dog is responding to. A calm, neutral cleanup prevents the appeasement cycle from reinforcing itself and avoids piling anxiety onto a situation that a dog cannot understand in retrospect.
  • Prevent the setup — If your dog keeps having accidents, consider more frequent potty breaks, a dog walker while you are at work, or crate training. If they keep chewing on inappropriate things, provide vigorous exercise before you leave and appropriate chew outlets or mentally stimulating toys for them to play with throughout the day.

When Something Bigger Is Going On

Persistent destructive behavior is not always a training issue. It can also be a sign of separation anxiety, which is a treatable condition that benefits from professional guidance.

If your dog only destroys things when left alone, if the destruction is combined with pacing, drooling, or vocalization, or if their distress seems to escalate when you leave, talk to your vet. A referral to a veterinary behaviorist can produce a tailored treatment plan for your pet. Also collaborate with your holistic veterinarian who may be able to provide calming herbal therapy, dog safe essential oils, and acupuncture treatments to help with separation anxiety.

Rethinking the Look on Their Face

Here is the reframe. That heartbreaking, apologetic little face is not a confession. It is a highly evolved social signal from an animal who is deeply attuned to you and desperate to keep the peace.

Your dog is not reviewing their choices from earlier in the day. They are not feeling remorse. They are not secretly plotting to be better next time. They are reading the storm cloud on your face and trying, in their sweet dog way, to make it go away.

Understanding this changes how you respond. When you meet the look with anger, you are punishing something the dog cannot connect to their earlier behavior. When you meet it calmly, you are telling the dog that their attempts to appease you have worked — and you are preserving the trust between you.

Poking fun at a guilty-looking dog in a viral video is one thing. Misinterpreting that look in real life can shape the relationship in ways nobody actually wants.

The Trickiest Face in the House

The guilty face works so well because it is designed to. Dogs became our closest companions in part because they are exceptional at reading and responding to human emotion. That skill is why we misread the look in the first place — it looks exactly like what human guilt looks like.

But under the hood, the mechanism is different. What you are seeing is a socially brilliant animal trying to smooth things over with the person they love most. That is not a confession. That’s connection.

Next time you walk into a room to find that classic look — the tucked tail, the sideways glance, the way they seem to melt into the floor — take a breath. Skip the lecture. Clean up the mess. And if you can, offer a little kindness. Your dog is not apologizing. They are asking if you are still their person. The answer, of course, is yes.

  • Averted eyes or refusal to make eye contact
  • A tucked tail (or a tail thumping the floor from a lowered posture)
  • Lip licking
  • Yawning
  • Whale eye (the whites of the eyes visible)
  • Hunched or lowered body posture
  • Cowering or retreating

These are all appeasement and stress signals. They are deeply ingrained social behaviors inherited from wolves, used to manage relationships and reduce social tension. When your dog senses that you are upset, tense, or angry, they use these signals in an attempt to calm the situation.

Dogs Are Reading You, Not Themselves

Here is what makes this so persuasive. Dogs are extraordinarily skilled at reading human body language, facial expressions, and tone of voice. Research has found they are actually better at reading us than our closest primate relatives are.10

When you walk into a room and your shoulders tense, your brow furrows, and your voice deepens, your dog notices it immediately. They notice the shift long before you have finished processing it consciously. The guilty look is their response to you — not to what they did an hour ago. It is a communication move, not a confession.

Every household has its own set of unwritten rules — what counts as “good” or “bad” behavior varies from home to home. Dogs come into these arrangements with no innate knowledge of your rules. They learn what you prefer through consistent training and consistent consequences, not through some inner moral compass. That is why the same dog can look “guilty” for something that would be perfectly acceptable in another home.11

Why the Look Develops

If the guilty look is not actual guilt, why does it come out so reliably in certain situations? The answer is classical and operant conditioning — the same learning mechanisms that shape most dog behavior.

Dogs are pattern-recognition experts. Over time, they learn to associate specific situations with specific outcomes. A dog who has been scolded for coming home to find a chewed-up cushion starts to associate coming home + chewed-up cushion + owner arriving with a negative reaction.

Crucially, the dog is not connecting their earlier chewing with the punishment. They are connecting the current environmental context (owner arriving, mess on floor) with what usually happens next (unpleasant interaction).

Over time, with repetition, that anticipation becomes a reliable, conditioned response. The guilty look then shows up preemptively any time those conditions are present — regardless of whether the dog has actually done anything wrong.

This helps explain some real-life head-scratchers. In multi-dog households, sometimes the guilty-looking dog is the innocent one — the peacemaker of the pair, who reads the tension and tries to de-escalate.12,13

Dogs Live in the Present

Another piece of the puzzle is time. Dogs live largely in the moment. They can have impressive memories for people, places, and trained behaviors, but their ability to consciously reflect on a past action and connect it to a delayed consequence is quite limited.

Studies on canine cognition suggest dogs have extremely limited deferred learning — meaning they struggle to link a consequence to an action that happened more than a few seconds earlier. The scold that happens two hours after the cushion was chewed simply does not connect back to the chewing in the dog's mind.

A dog who chewed a shoe two hours ago is not sitting in the corner thinking about it. They are doing dog things. Then you walk in, and their reaction is to your body language in the moment — not to the chewed shoe.14,15

Why After-the-Fact Punishment Backfires

This has real, practical consequences. Scolding your dog after the fact does not teach them not to chew shoes. It teaches them that their owner sometimes becomes unpredictably scary. That is the opposite of what most pet parents want.

Research on dog training outcomes has consistently shown that punishment-based methods are associated with increased anxiety, fear, and aggression — without producing reliable improvement in unwanted behavior.16

And there is a subtle side effect worth understanding. If you repeatedly react with anger to a mess (say, an accident on the rug), your dog learns to fear the presence of the mess itself. Some dogs start hiding accidents — eliminating in the basement or behind furniture — not because they know it is wrong, but because they have learned that your reaction to a visible mess is unpleasant.

Here’s What to Do Instead

Once you understand what the guilty look is, you can respond in ways that will help. Here are a few evidence-backed strategies:17,18,19

  • Focus on management first — Prevent access to the things your dog gets into. Crate training, baby gates, closed doors, and putting temptations out of reach do more than any correction can. Dogs cannot destroy what they cannot reach.
  • Only intervene if you catch them in the act — There is a two-second rule that helps: If you did not see it happen and cannot interrupt it in the moment, let it go. Redirecting a dog mid-behavior, such as offering an appropriate toy to chew and rewarding chewing on the toy, is far more effective than after-the-fact scolding.
  • Reinforce what you want — Positive reinforcement (rewarding desired behavior with treats, praise, or play) is the most effective and least harmful method of shaping dog behavior. Rather than focusing on what your dog did wrong, focus on building the habits you want them to have.
  • Supervise, then interrupt calmly — When your dog is wandering and eyeing something they should not have, gently interrupt them before it becomes a chase. A shake of a treat bag, a squeaked toy, a friendly call — all followed by a reward when they redirect to you.
  • Stay calm when you find a mess — This is often the hardest part. Try to remember that your emotional response is what your dog is responding to. A calm, neutral cleanup prevents the appeasement cycle from reinforcing itself and avoids piling anxiety onto a situation that a dog cannot understand in retrospect.
  • Prevent the setup — If your dog keeps having accidents, consider more frequent potty breaks, a dog walker while you are at work, or crate training. If they keep chewing on inappropriate things, provide vigorous exercise before you leave and appropriate chew outlets or mentally stimulating toys for them to play with throughout the day.

When Something Bigger Is Going On

Persistent destructive behavior is not always a training issue. It can also be a sign of separation anxiety, which is a treatable condition that benefits from professional guidance.

If your dog only destroys things when left alone, if the destruction is combined with pacing, drooling, or vocalization, or if their distress seems to escalate when you leave, talk to your vet. A referral to a veterinary behaviorist can produce a tailored treatment plan for your pet. Also collaborate with your holistic veterinarian who may be able to provide calming herbal therapy, dog safe essential oils, and acupuncture treatments to help with separation anxiety.

Rethinking the Look on Their Face

Here is the reframe. That heartbreaking, apologetic little face is not a confession. It is a highly evolved social signal from an animal who is deeply attuned to you and desperate to keep the peace.

Your dog is not reviewing their choices from earlier in the day. They are not feeling remorse. They are not secretly plotting to be better next time. They are reading the storm cloud on your face and trying, in their sweet dog way, to make it go away.

Understanding this changes how you respond. When you meet the look with anger, you are punishing something the dog cannot connect to their earlier behavior. When you meet it calmly, you are telling the dog that their attempts to appease you have worked — and you are preserving the trust between you.

Poking fun at a guilty-looking dog in a viral video is one thing. Misinterpreting that look in real life can shape the relationship in ways nobody actually wants.

The Trickiest Face in the House

The guilty face works so well because it is designed to. Dogs became our closest companions in part because they are exceptional at reading and responding to human emotion. That skill is why we misread the look in the first place — it looks exactly like what human guilt looks like.

But under the hood, the mechanism is different. What you are seeing is a socially brilliant animal trying to smooth things over with the person they love most. That is not a confession. That’s connection.

Next time you walk into a room to find that classic look — the tucked tail, the sideways glance, the way they seem to melt into the floor — take a breath. Skip the lecture. Clean up the mess. And if you can, offer a little kindness. Your dog is not apologizing. They are asking if you are still their person. The answer, of course, is yes.
